source: The eight shared exercises, in the shape of the Greek shared file. Answer strings that the Latin exercise fixes are copied exactly. French has no case on the noun, so the case items ask for the pronoun form, and one government item states that the noun has no case.

pos.note: Le points out the king. French has a definite article, and Latin has none.
Le points out the book. The article agrees with livre, which is masculine and singular.
Roi names the king, and it is the subject of parle.
Cheval names the horse, and it is the object of vend.
Parle says what the king does. It is the present, third person singular, of parler.
Finit says what the woman does. It is the present, third person singular, of finir.
Bon tells what sort of king, and it agrees with roi.
Belle tells what sort of woman, and it agrees with femme.
Bien tells how he speaks. The adverb keeps one form.
Souvent tells how often he comes. The adverb keeps one form.
Dans stands before the noun and marks the place. The noun itself does not change.
Avec stands before the noun and marks the company. The noun itself does not change.

pos.orig: The king and the woman speak.
pos.note: Et joins the two nouns. The verb is plural because the subject is the two of them.

pos.s: Le roi parle, mais la femme finit.
pos.orig: The king speaks, but the woman finishes.
pos.note: Mais joins the two statements and marks the contrast.
Il stands for a masculine subject. Latin would often leave the pronoun out.
Le stands for the thing sold, and no noun follows it, so it is a pronoun and not the article.
Parlé is the past participle of parler. With a it makes the passé composé.

pos.s: La femme, parlant au roi, finit le livre.
pos.orig: The woman, speaking to the king, finishes the book.
pos.note: Parlant is the present participle of parler. It stands beside the finite verb finit.
Hélas is a cry, and it keeps one form.
Ah is a cry, and it keeps one form.

cases.q: What form is the marked pronoun?
ds: Direct-object form
Indirect-object form
Stressed form
cases.why: Je is the subject of parle, so the pronoun is in the subject form. The object form is me, and the stressed form is moi.

cases.q: What form is the marked pronoun?
ds: Direct-object form
Indirect-object form
Stressed form
cases.why: Elle is the subject of finit, so the pronoun is in the subject form. After a preposition the same letters are the stressed form, and there is no preposition here.

cases.q: What form is the marked pronoun?
ds: Subject form
Indirect-object form
Stressed form
cases.why: Le is the thing sold, and it is the direct object of vend. The pronoun stands before the verb.

cases.q: What form is the marked pronoun?
ds: Subject form
Indirect-object form
Stressed form
cases.why: Les is the thing finished, and it is plural. It is the direct object of finit, and it stands before the verb.

cases.q: What form is the marked pronoun?
ds: Subject form
Indirect-object form
Stressed form
cases.why: L’ is le or la before the vowel of a. It is the direct object of a, from avoir, and it stands before the verb.

cases.q: What form is the marked pronoun?
ds: Subject form
Direct-object form
Stressed form
cases.why: Parler takes à for the person spoken to. When that person is a pronoun before the verb, the form is lui, the indirect object. Lui here is not the stressed pronoun, because no preposition is written.

cases.q: What form is the marked pronoun?
ds: Subject form
Direct-object form
Stressed form
cases.why: Leur is the indirect object, plural, of parle. The person spoken to would be marked by à if the noun were written out.

cases.q: What form is the marked pronoun?
ds: Subject form
Direct-object form
Indirect-object form
cases.why: Avec is a preposition, and the pronoun after it is the stressed form. Moi is that form. Je cannot stand there.

cases.q: What form is the marked pronoun?
ds: Subject form
Direct-object form
Indirect-object form
cases.why: Eux is the stressed form, masculine plural, after the preposition avec. The subject form would be ils.

cases.q: What form is the marked pronoun?
ds: Subject form
Direct-object form
Indirect-object form
cases.why: After c’est the pronoun is the stressed form. Toi is that form, and tu is the subject form.

govern.q: What form does avec require of the pronoun?
ds: Subject form
Direct-object form
Indirect-object form
govern.why: Avec is a preposition, so the pronoun is the stressed form. Moi is that form. Je is the subject form, and it does not stand after avec.

govern.q: What form does pour require of the pronoun?
ds: Subject form
Direct-object form
Indirect-object form
govern.why: Pour is a preposition, so the pronoun is the stressed form. Toi is that form, and tu is the subject form.

govern.q: What form does sans require of the pronoun?
ds: Subject form
Direct-object form
Indirect-object form
govern.why: Sans is a preposition, so the pronoun is the stressed form. Elle is spelled like the subject form, and the use after the preposition is still the stressed one. Il would not stand there.

govern.q: What form does parler à take when the pronoun stands before the verb?
ds: Subject form
Direct-object form
Stressed form after a preposition
govern.why: Parler à marks the person spoken to. Before the verb that person is lui, the indirect object. The stressed form would follow a written preposition, and this sentence has none.

govern.q: What form does vendre à take for the buyer, when the pronoun stands before the verb?
ds: Subject form
Direct-object form
Stressed form after a preposition
govern.why: Vendre à marks the buyer. Before the verb the buyer is leur, the indirect object. Le livre is the thing sold, and it stays a noun here.

govern.q: What form does finir take for the thing finished?
ds: Subject form
Indirect-object form
Stressed form
govern.why: The thing finished is the direct object. Le stands for it and stands before finit. Lui would be a person spoken to, which finir does not take in this sentence.

govern.q: What form does avoir take for the thing had?
ds: Subject form
Indirect-object form
Stressed form
govern.why: The thing had is the direct object of a. L’ is that pronoun before a vowel. Avoir does not put the thing had in a stressed form.

govern.q: What case does dans give the noun?
ds: Dative
The accusative, as Latin uses for motion
The ablative, as Latin uses for place where
govern.why: Dans marks the place, and ville does not change its form. French does not put the noun in the accusative for motion or in the ablative for place. Latin in does make that difference.

agree.a: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
ds: Faulty: the adjective disagrees in gender
Faulty: the number does not agree
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Roi is masculine and singular. Bon is the masculine singular, so the adjective agrees. French marks no case on either word.

agree.a: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
ds: Faulty: the adjective disagrees in gender
Faulty: the number does not agree
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Femme is feminine and singular. Belle is the feminine singular of beau, so the adjective agrees.

agree.a: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
ds: Faulty: the adjective disagrees in gender
Faulty: the number does not agree
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Chevaux is masculine and plural. Beaux is the masculine plural of beau, so the adjective agrees.

agree.a: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
ds: Faulty: the adjective disagrees in gender
Faulty: the number does not agree
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Ami is masculine and singular, and it begins with a vowel. Vieil is the masculine singular of vieux used before a vowel, so the adjective agrees. Lawless requires that form.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the number does not agree
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Femme is feminine. Bon is masculine, so the adjective disagrees in gender. Both words are singular, and French marks no case here.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the number does not agree
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Roi is masculine. Belle is feminine, so the adjective disagrees in gender. Number is singular on both words.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the number does not agree
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Femme is feminine. Heureux is the masculine form, and the feminine is heureuse, so the adjective disagrees in gender.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the number does not agree
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Table is feminine. Petit is masculine, and the feminine is petite, so the adjective disagrees in gender.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective disagrees in gender
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Rois is plural. Bon is singular, and the masculine plural is bons, so the number does not agree. Both words are masculine.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective disagrees in gender
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Cheval is singular. Beaux is plural, so the number does not agree. Both words are masculine.

produce.why: The plural of roi adds s. The singular is roi.
The plural of cheval is chevaux. The stem changes, and the ending is x.
The plural of cadeau is cadeaux. A noun in -eau takes -x.
The feminine of ami is amie. The article before it is l’, because the word begins with a vowel.
The feminine singular of bon is bonne. The n is doubled.

produce.want: masculine singular used before a vowel
produce.why: Before a masculine noun that begins with a vowel, beau becomes bel. Larousse gives bel as that form.
The feminine plural of vieux is vieilles.
The feminine singular of heureux is heureuse. The masculine plural stays heureux.
Parlons is the present, first person plural, of parler. The subject pronoun is nous.
Parlait is the imparfait, third person singular. The present subjunctive is parle, so the two are not the same spelling.
Parleront is the future, third person plural. The stem is the infinitive, and the ending is -ont.
Parler takes avoir. The third person singular is a parlé. The participle does not agree with the subject. The written subject is il or elle, and je would be written j’.
Finissait is the imparfait, third person singular. The present is finit, and the present subjunctive is finisse, so this spelling belongs to the imparfait.
Finisse is the present subjunctive, third person singular. The present indicative is finit, so the mood is visible in the spelling.
Vend is the present, third person singular. No letter is added to the stem.
Sommes is the present, first person plural, of être. The subject pronoun is nous.
Soient is the present subjunctive, third person plural. The indicative is sont.
Aie is the present subjunctive, first person singular, of avoir. The indicative is ai. Que is written with it: que j’aie. The imperative uses the same spelling, and it is not asked.
Vais is the present, first person singular, of aller. The stem is va-, and the infinitive stem all- is not used here.

produce.want: passé composé, third person singular feminine
produce.why: Aller takes être, so the participle agrees with a feminine singular subject. The form is est allée. The masculine in the same person is est allé.

Faites is the present, second person plural, of faire. The form is not faisez. The subject pronoun vous takes this ending whether vous means one person or more than one. The feminine plural of the participle is spelled the same way, and this item asks the present.

produce.want: passé composé, third person plural feminine
produce.why: Venir takes être, so the participle agrees. The feminine plural is sont venues. The masculine or mixed plural is sont venus.

cong.a: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
ds: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: The article fits the noun, and the noun and the verb fit. A finite verb makes the sentence complete.

cong.s: La femme a fini le livre.
cong.a: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
ds: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: The parts fit, and the passé composé is a finite verb, so the sentence is complete. Whether she has in fact finished is not asked.

cong.a: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
ds: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: Les agrees with chevaux, and sont venus agrees with that plural masculine subject. The sentence is complete.

cong.a: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
ds: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: The pronoun, the verb, and the object fit, and a finite verb finishes the sentence.

cong.a: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: Bon fits roi, and le fits roi. There is no verb, so the sense is not yet complete.

cong.a: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: Belle fits ville. There is no verb, so the sense is not yet complete.

cong.a: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: Heureuse fits femme. There is no verb, so the sense is not yet complete.

cong.a: Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
cong.why: Roi is singular and parlent is plural. The parts do not fit. Parlent is a real form, and the fault is the join.

cong.a: Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
cong.why: Femme is feminine and le is masculine. The parts do not fit. Each word is a French form, and the fault is the join.

vices.a: Barbarism: a form French does not have
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Parlont is not a form of parler. The third person plural of the present is parlent. The fault is in the one word.

vices.a: Barbarism: a form French does not have
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Chevals is not the plural of cheval. The plural is chevaux. Viennent is a real form, and the fault is in the one noun.

vices.a: Barbarism: a form French does not have
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Finisons is not a form of finir. The first person plural of the present is finissons. The fault is in the one word.

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Les is a real plural article, and femme is a real singular noun. The two do not agree in number. Parlent fits les, and the fault is the join of les and femme.

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Je is a real subject form, and avec is a real preposition. A preposition takes the stressed form, which is moi. The fault is the join.

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Parlons is a real first person plural. The subject roi is third person singular, so the verb does not fit it.

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Beau and ami are both real forms. Before a masculine singular noun that begins with a vowel, the form is bel. Lawless says that special form is required. The fault is the join.
